clinicalPearls: An inflammation of subcutaneous fat provoked by mechanical injury, blunt trauma, pressure or repetitive friction, producing tender nodules or plaques at the site of insult.
Common sites reflect exposure to trauma: the breasts, thighs, buttocks and shins; a history of a precipitating event is often but not always elicited.
Cold-related and pressure-related forms overlap clinically; the breast is a classic site where post-traumatic fat necrosis can mimic carcinoma.
Lesions evolve from firm tender nodules to indurated, sometimes fibrotic or calcified masses, and may become mobile and encapsulated over time.
Histology shows a mostly lobular panniculitis with fat necrosis, lipophages (foamy macrophages), lipomembranous (membranocystic) change and later fibrosis.
Imaging of breast lesions may reveal an oil cyst with rim calcification, a helpful clue to a benign traumatic aetiology.
Diagnosis rests on correlating a clear mechanical history with compatible histology after excluding infective and systemic panniculitides.
Most lesions are self-limiting and resolve with conservative care; the main clinical imperative is to avoid mistaking them for malignancy.
reference.pathophysiology: Mechanical trauma, sustained pressure or repetitive friction disrupts adipocytes and their vascular supply, releasing intracellular lipid into the interstitium. Free triglycerides are hydrolysed by tissue lipases into free fatty acids, which incite a lobular inflammatory response dominated by lipophagic macrophages that engulf the liberated lipid. Ischaemia from injured vessels contributes to fat necrosis. Over time the infiltrate gives way to foreign-body granulomas, lipomembranous change and fibrosis, with occasional dystrophic calcification and oil-cyst formation. In the breast this reparative fibrosis can produce a firm, spiculated mass that clinically and radiologically simulates carcinoma.
additionalInvestigations: deep incisional or excisional biopsy including subcutaneous fat for histopathology
ultrasound or mammography for breast lesions (oil cyst, rim calcification)
tissue cultures to exclude infection when clinically indicated
MRI for deep or diagnostically uncertain lesions
core biopsy of suspicious breast masses to exclude malignancy
review of medication and occupational or activity history for repetitive trauma
redFlags: a firm, fixed or enlarging breast mass that cannot be confidently distinguished from carcinoma
systemic features (fever, weight loss) suggesting infection or an alternative systemic panniculitis
ulceration or discharge raising concern for infection or factitial disease
absence of any plausible traumatic history prompting a search for another cause
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and usually self-limiting, resolving over weeks to months, though residual fibrosis, calcification or an encapsulated fatty nodule may persist.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting a post-traumatic breast mass as carcinoma, or vice versa, without appropriate imaging and biopsy.
Accepting a trivial or coincidental trauma history and overlooking a systemic panniculitis.
Sampling too superficially and missing the lobular fat pathology.
Assuming all fat necrosis is traumatic and failing to consider pancreatic or infective causes.
Attributing recurrent lesions to trauma when factitial disease is responsible.
references: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, current edition
Fitzpatrick's Dermatology in General Medicine, current edition
management: Conservative management with analgesia, warm compresses and rest, as the panniculitis is self-limiting
Identify and remove the precipitating mechanical cause, whether blunt trauma, sustained pressure or repetitive friction
Exclude malignancy in breast lesions that mimic carcinoma, using mammography or ultrasound and core biopsy where imaging is suspicious
Confirm the diagnosis with deep incisional or excisional biopsy including subcutaneous fat in atypical or uncertain lesions
Reassure that lesions resolve over weeks to months, while explaining that residual fibrosis, calcification or an encapsulated fatty nodule may persist
